outputs.L1:
Startled from its snow-day slumber by a neighbor’s mutt, it banged its buzzard’s head, then couldn’t solve the problem of the white pine’s limbs, its wings nearly too broad for the planned descent. Somewhere, an awkward angel knows whether it was dead before it hit the ground. Any sinner could tell it was dead afterward—eyes unseen beneath bare, wrinkled lids; feet drawn up almost as high as hands.

I loved to watch thistle and millet disappear beneath it in the yard. As snow covers feathers that will still be iridescent in spring, I remember seeing a businessman take a dripping handful of pocket change and throw it down a subway grate beside a homeless man. The coins bounced and clattered, vanishing into the humid dark. The rich man said, “Now you’re having a shitty day too.”

But it is not a shitty day, and it will not be when I retrieve the bird and walk it—toes curling stiffly from a shopping bag—to a houseless scrap of oak savannah that birdseed drew it from, then dig it into deeper snow so that, by the thaw, what was hoarded by a man may be doled out.
outputs.L2:
A neighbor’s dog jolted it awake on a snowy day; in the commotion, the bird struck its vulturine head and found itself trapped among the white pine’s branches, its wings almost too wide for the downward route it meant to take. Only some clumsy angel could say if life left it before the fall. Afterward, though, even the wicked knew it was dead: naked, creased eyelids concealed its eyes, and its feet were tucked nearly level with its hands.

I used to delight in watching it consume the thistle and millet scattered across the yard. Now snow settles over plumage that will remain rainbow-bright come spring, and I think of a businessman I once saw scoop up a wet fistful of coins and fling them through a subway grate next to an unhoused man. The change ricocheted with a metallic racket before disappearing into the damp darkness. “Now you’re having a shitty day too,” the wealthy man said.

Yet this day is not shitty, nor will it become so when I collect the bird, carry it with its rigid toes hooking around a shopping bag, and return it to the homeless remnant of oak savannah from which the birdseed had lured it. There I will bury it beneath thicker snow, so that when the thaw arrives, what one man amassed may finally be distributed.
outputs.L3:
Startled and disoriented, a bird struggles to find its way through the snow-covered branches of a white pine. In its panic, it strikes its head and dies. The speaker remembers seeing the same bird alive in the yard, quietly feeding on thistle and millet.

As the snow gradually covers the bird’s body, another troubling image comes to mind: a businessman tossing coins down a subway grate beside a homeless man, turning an apparent act of generosity into one of deliberate cruelty. Yet despite the bird’s death and this reminder of human callousness, the speaker refuses to declare the day entirely bad.

Instead, the speaker chooses to perform a small act of care. The bird will be buried deep in the snow, along with the food it had hoarded. When the snow thaws, those seeds may nourish the oak savannah, allowing something new to grow from the bird’s death and offering a quiet sense of renewal.
outputs.L4:
Here is an original expanded version:

The bird lay on the snow as if it had been dropped there by the cold itself. Its wings were folded close to its body, and its dark feathers made a small, precise mark against the white. Nothing around it had been disturbed. There were no tracks leading toward it, no signs of struggle, only the faint hollow where its weight had pressed into the crust. I stood over it for a long time, noticing the delicate curve of its beak, the closed lids, the feet drawn inward as though even in death it had tried to preserve a little warmth.

Snow had stranded it between seasons. The earth was sealed beneath ice, and the insects and seeds that might once have fed it were buried. Now the bird itself could not return to the ground. It rested on the frozen surface, exposed and useless, while the wind moved loose crystals over its feathers.

Looking at it, I remembered a man I had seen years before outside a train station. He was sitting beneath the awning with his back against the brick, wrapped in a coat too thin for the weather. A paper cup stood beside his shoe. As people passed, he asked quietly for change. Most pretended not to hear.

A group of young men came out of a nearby bar, loud with drink and confidence. One of them stopped, bent toward the seated man, and held out a coin. When the man reached for it, the stranger pulled his hand away. His friends laughed. He offered the coin again, then withdrew it again, turning need into entertainment. I watched from across the street. I remember my disgust, but I also remember that I did nothing. I kept walking.

That memory returned beside the bird because death is not the only form of abandonment. Sometimes suffering becomes part of the scenery. We look at it, name it unfortunate, and continue on our way. We protect ourselves by believing that what has fallen is separate from us.

I could not help the man then—or, more truthfully, I chose not to—but I could lift the bird now.

Its body was almost weightless in my gloved hands. I carried it beyond the path to the oak savannah, where the trees stood widely spaced beneath the winter sky. There, last summer’s grasses leaned through the snow, and the black limbs of the oaks reached outward with patient strength. I found a sheltered place near the base of one tree and brushed aside the loose snow. The ground beneath was still frozen, so I laid the bird among the grasses and covered it lightly with leaves.

The gesture did not undo its death. It did not redeem my earlier silence or answer the larger question of why living things suffer. Yet it returned the bird to a place where death would not remain merely an ending. When the thaw came, insects would find it. Its feathers would loosen. Its body would enter the soil, feeding roots, grasses, fungi, and perhaps the oak itself. What had seemed stranded would become part of the world again.

I stood there imagining spring: water moving beneath the ice, green shoots rising through the flattened leaves, birds calling from the branches overhead. The small body would disappear, but not into nothingness. It would be given away.

Then I walked back through the snow with empty hands. Grief remained, as did shame, but both felt altered. I could not prevent every death or repair every cruelty. I could, however, refuse to leave this one creature exposed on the indifferent white. I could carry it to a place where the earth, once open, would receive it.
outputs.L5: Startled by a sudden knock, Mara froze in the darkened hallway. Somewhere beyond the window, a dog began to bark, and the wind carried the faint sound of footsteps. She reached for the lamp, wondering whether any light would make her feel safer—or reveal what was waiting outside.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about finding a dead pigeon after it crashes into a white pine on a snowy morning, weaving in bird feeding, mortality, and a disturbing memory of a businessman humiliating a homeless man.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the pigeon lies beneath the white pine as if the tree has shaken loose a gray, unfinished thought. Snow cups the body without warmth. One wing is folded correctly, the other keeps its last argument with the sky. Above it, the trunk bears no wound, only a dusting of powder and the green needles holding their small dark weather.

I had come out with seed in a coffee tin—millet, cracked corn, black suns of sunflower—thinking hunger was a simple door I could open. Chickadees stitched the air between my hands and the hedge. Sparrows waited in the bare lilac, each heart a bead of urgency. I scattered breakfast over the snow, and the living descended beside the dead, cautious at first, then busy, because winter permits no long ceremony.

The pigeon’s eye was closed. That mercy undid me. I remembered a businessman outside the station years ago, his polished shoes planted wide while he made a homeless man kneel for a dollar. People slowed, then hurried. The businessman laughed as if money had invented gravity. The man’s hands trembled near the wet pavement; his face became a place the rest of us refused to enter. I did not stop it. All morning afterward, my silence rode inside me like a black elevator, descending.

Now the feeders sway from the pine, each one a little public promise. Take what you need. No bowing. No gratitude performed for the full. Snow gathers on the pigeon’s back until death resembles shelter, though it is not shelter. I lift the bird with both hands, surprised by how light the ended world can be, how the body that struck the tree contains no accusation, only feathers, cooling muscle, the hush after impact.

Around me, beaks tap the frozen seed. The pine stands white and blameless. Somewhere, men are counting money; somewhere, someone is hungry enough to accept humiliation as bread. I carry the pigeon beyond the feeding place and lay it under the low boughs, where the snow is shallow. Then I return to the tin and pour out everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, single-paragraph elegy for an urban bird killed during an awkward landing. Use dark humor, religious imagery, vivid physical detail, and end with the speaker returning the bird’s hoarded seed to nature.
counterfactuals.output: He came down wrong on the laundromat awning, our gray apostle of gutters, one wing still preaching while the other folded beneath him like a broken umbrella, his small red feet clutching at nothing, his breast ticking once, twice, then quitting the shift; above, the traffic lights changed with bureaucratic mercy, and a bus sighed at the curb as if Heaven had dispatched public transit for his soul. Up close he was all oil-slick throat, rain-dark feathers, and one bright eye reflecting the pawnshop cross, ridiculous saint of french fries and cigarette ash, martyred not by hawk or storm but by bad angles and aluminum siding—the city’s cheapest crucifixion. I found beneath his tongue and in the warm little purse of his crop a miser’s treasury: millet, cracked corn, two sunflower hearts, enough provisions for a resurrection that would not be scheduled. So I carried him to the vacant lot where weeds lifted their ragged congregation, laid him under the billboard’s false blue heaven, and, with my thumb, scattered his hoarded seed back into the earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental winter poem in the style of contemporary ecopoetry: a dog startles a sleeping narrator, a pigeon dies in the snow, and the event recalls coins being thrown down a subway grate beside a houseless person.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cold Ledger**

At 3:17 the dog detonates—  
four paws against the bed,  
a bark dragged in from weather.

I wake inside my animal body:  
heart, small fist; breath, white flag.  
Beyond the glass, snow edits the street  
until every parked car  
pretends it was never oil.

The dog insists.

Under the cedar, a pigeon  
has folded itself into the grammar of winter—  
gray wing, red comma,  
one eye holding  
the blank sky accountable.

No movement except snow  
entering feather  
entering silence  
entering the municipal drain.

And suddenly: the subway grate, July,  
coins flung down for luck—  
quarters flashing past  
the person sleeping beside the heat,  
their cardboard sign bending  
in the train-breath.

How easily we feed  
the metal mouth beneath them.

How the coins rang once,  
then vanished into infrastructure,  
small moons no hand could reach.

The dog noses the dead bird.  
I call her back.

Above us, carbon keeps its books  
in rings of ice,  
in salt-burned roots,  
in the pigeon’s cooling crop  
full of our crumbs.

Snow covers nothing.  
Snow is a page that keeps  
taking dictation:

  body / body / grate / wing  
  mercy misplaced as currency  
  warmth rising through iron  
  to no one’s name

Morning arrives without absolution.

I lift the bird with a shovel.  
The dog watches, trembling  
at what refuses to wake.

Somewhere under the city  
the coins remain bright,  
having purchased  
nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense prose poem that moves associatively between a dead bird beneath a white pine, the narrator’s pleasure in watching it eat thistle and millet, an act of cruelty witnessed in a subway, and a final gesture of burial in an oak savannah.
counterfactuals.output: Beneath the white pine the bird lay as if the wind had misplaced a small gray glove, one wing unbuttoned, the black seed of its eye refusing the sky. Yesterday—or every day before death learned its address—I watched it at the feeder, pleased by the brisk arithmetic of hunger: thistle, millet, thistle, the beak clicking shut on each pale syllable, the husks falling like minute declarations of snow. Pleasure is a kind of witness, though witness is not mercy. On the subway a man ground his boot onto a beetle-colored pigeon that had wandered through the open doors, and when the bird battered itself against the yellow seats, everyone became suddenly devout before their phones; only a child cried out, his voice thin as a feather’s shaft, while the man smiled with the calm of someone tightening a lid. The train entered darkness. The pine needles entered the dead bird’s breast. I carried it later in my two hands, its body lighter than the shame of having hands, past the last houses to the oak savannah where the trees stood far apart, keeping their old, golden counsel. There I opened the earth with a stone, laid beside it a pinch of thistle and millet—not food, not forgiveness, merely the grammar of what I had loved—and covered the bird until the ground was level, then pressed my palm to the soil as if waiting for a small heart to answer from beneath it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a melancholic but unsentimental poem about retrieving a frozen bird in a shopping bag and burying it in deep snow. Include iridescent feathers, curled toes, social inequality, scavenging or hoarding, and the possibility that stored food will be redistributed after the thaw.
counterfactuals.output:
I carried the frozen bird home  
in a shopping bag,  
its iridescent feathers dimming  
from green to oil-black  
whenever the plastic turned.

Its toes were curled  
around the absence of a branch.  
There was no blood,  
only the clean arithmetic of cold.

Behind the houses, snow lay deep  
over gardens and locked sheds,  
over bins where some of us scavenge  
and cellars where others hoard  
flour, tins, winter apples—  
each hunger assigned its address.

I dug with a broken spade  
until the white became blue,  
then set the bird down  
still shaped for flight  
and covered it without ceremony.

By spring, the drifts will loosen.  
Mice may find the buried grain,  
crows split open forgotten sacks,  
meltwater carry seed downhill.

What was stored against the poor  
may yet be redistributed—  
not by mercy, not by law,  
but by thaw, rot, root,  
and the small, impartial mouths  
that survive us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
